title: Spatially Gated Demographic Steering for Debiasing Multi-Person Text-to-Image Generation

paper.title: Spatially Gated Demographic Steering for Debiasing Multi-Person Text-to-Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Text-to-Image models reproduce societal stereotypes, and existing mitigation applies one demographic correction to the whole scene.
In multi-person scene generation this creates a trade-off: global steering improves aggregate balance only by homogenizing the people within an image.
Steering-based methods like Embedding Arithmetic drive the intra-image diversity below the unsteered baseline.
Text- and latent-projection approaches shift the aggregate skew with only marginal gains in intra-image diversity.
We present Spatially Gated Steering (SGS), which steers the demographics of each person independently by extracting per-person masks from the Diffusion Transformer’s (DiT) internal attention maps at a critical denoising timestep and applying a distinct demographic vector within each mask for the remaining steps.
SGS needs no fine-tuning, inversion or layout specifications, and uses a lightweight segmentor over frozen DiT attention features to localize subjects at early timesteps.
On skewed occupational prompts, SGS reaches high intra-image racial and gender diversity while keeping aggregate balance competitive and image quality near baseline, a result we validate on two architecturally distinct diffusion transformers, FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Large.
Codebase and model weights are available at https://github.com/cvims/spatially-gated-steering

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-Image (T2I) generation has transformed digital content creation, yet foundational models such as FLUX [ 24 ] and Stable Diffusion [ 10 ] systematically reproduce societal stereotypes [ 9 ] . Gender-neutral prompts like a carpenter yield predominantly male-presenting images; a nurse yields predominantly female-presenting images [ 28 ] . Studies show these outputs shift user beliefs about real-world distributions [ 14 ] , making fairness mitigation essential for responsible deployment. Figure 1 : SGS intuition. The base trajectory (black) reaches x 0 base x_{0}^{\text{base}} in a stereotyped region of p data p_{\text{data}} ; global mitigation [ 39 ] (brown dashed) shifts it to one alternative mode. SGS instead intercepts at x start x_{\text{start}} , extracts per-person masks, and steers each individual independently (orange/blue dashed) toward distinct demographic attractors within the same image x 0 x_{0} . Several mitigation strategies have been proposed and they operate at different levels of the diffusion pipeline [ 37 ] : They modify the text embeddings [ 39 , 6 , 43 , 22 ] or fine-tune model weights [ 13 , 36 ] to shift the aggregate output distribution. While effective for scenes with a single person, global mitigation methods share a fundamental limitation: They apply identical steering to every person in a scene. A prompt like ”a group of nurses” receives one demographic vector, pushing all the persons in the image in the same direction and failing to diversify individuals independently. Figure 2 : Qualitative comparison across three profession types spanning different stereotype directions. Prompts contain no demographic descriptors. Base is demographically homogeneous; EA shifts everyone uniformly; FairImagen is statistically indistinguishable from baseline on FLUX; SGS steers each instance toward a distinct intersectional target while preserving occupational context and scene coherence. Rightmost column: segmentation masks (nearest-neighbor upsampled from 32 × 32 32\times 32 ) with assigned demographic labels. This limitation is not merely theoretical: Wan and Chang [41] show that multi-person prompts expose a distinct, compounding class of bias that single-subject evaluations cannot capture. Co-occurring subjects amplify stereotypes even when the same model behaves anti-stereotypically on single-person prompts. Attempts to address this gap remain limited. Existing approaches either rewrite the generation prompt with a single corrective signal applied to the whole scene [ 41 , 8 ] , optimize demographic distributions at the aggregate level without per-instance control [ 18 ] , or require an explicit spatial layout as input [ 7 ] . To the best of our knowledge, no existing method localizes individuals from the model’s own internal representations and applies independent demographic steering, to achieve intra-image diversity. Figure 1 illustrates this gap: while global mitigation shifts all persons uniformly toward a single demographic mode, our approach steers each individual independently through their spatial mask, reaching distinct attractors within p data p_{\text{data}} in a single denoising pass. We introduce Spatially Gated Steering (SGS) , a framework for per-instance demographic steering in multi-person T2I scene generation. SGS operates by 1) Identifying and generating the masks of instances of people during the intermediate denoising steps using a lightweight detector, 2) Steering the demographics of the detected individuals, while also maintaining concept coherence. Our contributions are as follows: • A trade-off in multi-person fairness. Global mitigation faces an inherent tension: improving aggregate balance requires collapsing intra-image diversity, sometimes below the unsteered baseline. Since any per-instance diversification trivially raises intra-image entropy, the meaningful result is high entropy at a competitive aggregate balance. SGS reaches high intra-image diversity with a competitive aggregate balance by steering per-instance without fine-tuning, flow-inversion or layout. • Instance segmentation from DiT features. We show that self-attention maps of DiTs at a critical denoising timestep encode spatially separable person instances, and train a lightweight DETR-style [ 4 ] segmentor on these frozen features that isolates individuals across crowd sizes and scene complexities. • Benchmark and analysis. We introduce a benchmark measuring fairness along both intra-image diversity and aggregate deviation, surfacing the homogenization failure mode of global methods and showing SGS is strong on both axes, on both FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Large.

sections.heading: Bias and Fairness in Text-to-Image Models.
sections.text: T2I models have been extensively shown to amplify demographic stereotypes encoded in training data, producing outputs skewed by gender, race and cultural identity across a wide range of prompt types [ 1 , 5 , 35 , 28 ] . Beyond documenting these skews, a parallel line of work formalizes their measurement: Dehdashtian et al. [ 9 ] quantify stereotypical attributes in the generated set and trace their origin within the model, reporting that even high-fidelity systems such as FLUX retain strong stereotypical predispositions. Mitigation strategies operate at different points in the generation pipeline: prompt engineering injects demographic descriptors at inference [ 11 , 2 , 43 ] , embedding manipulation steers text representations prior to image generation [ 39 , 6 , 22 , 25 , 26 , 15 ] , and parameter-efficient fine-tuning edits model weights to shift output distributions [ 13 , 36 ] . Park et al.’s Entanglement-Free Attention [ 30 ] shares our goal of preserving non-target attributes during bias mitigation, training cross-attention predictors under a mask-constrained regularization loss so background edits are suppressed. However, like other global methods, it applies one scene-level attribute correction rather than steering each person independently. Despite this breadth, all existing methods treat the generated image as a single unit, applying one steering signal to the entire scene. This is sufficient when a prompt produces one person, but breaks down entirely for multi-person scenes where distinct individuals require independent control.

sections.heading: Multi-person Bias and Instance-level Control.
sections.text: This breakdown in multi-subject generation is primarily driven by semantic leakage, a phenomenon where the attention mechanisms of diffusion architectures inadvertently blend the visual and demographic features of different subjects during the denoising trajectory. Wan and Chang [41] demonstrate the consequences of this at scale: their Paired Stereotype Test shows that over 74% of DALL-E 3 images depicting two individuals with contrastive social identities display gender-occupational biases, even when the same model produces anti-stereotypical outputs for single-person prompts. Jung et al. [18] propose a Multi-Group Proportional Representation metric to measure and optimize demographic distributions across intersectional groups, but operate at the aggregate level without per-instance control. A related direction targets stereotypes that emerge from the co-occurrence of multiple concepts within a single prompt: Zhou et al. [47] show that pairing a demographic descriptor with an unrelated object can induce stereotypical associations invisible to single-concept audits, mitigated via a trained Sensitive Transformer that constrains the output distribution toward a stereotype-free target. This targets a distinct problem from ours, stereotyped associations between a subject and its surrounding context, corrected globally over the whole generation, rather than diversifying multiple people already explicitly present in a scene. Training-free inference methods such as Bounded Attention [ 7 ] attempt to prevent semantic leakage by confining attention flows within manually predefined spatial bounding boxes, but rely on rigid user-provided layouts rather than organic scene composition. Reinforcement learning approaches such as DisCo [ 3 ] directly fine-tune models to penalize intra-image facial similarity, but use face similarity as a proxy for demographic diversity rather than steering specific attribute vectors, and incur significant computational overhead. Global steering techniques such as Embedding Arithmetic [ 39 ] modify text embeddings uniformly, which fundamentally fails to produce heterogeneous intra-image diversity.

sections.heading: Diffusion Features for Spatial Understanding.
sections.text: Intermediate diffusion activations encode rich spatial structure without additional training: DIFT [ 38 ] shows mid-denoising U-Net features support zero-shot dense correspondence; ODISE [ 42 ] uses Stable Diffusion U-Net features for open-vocabulary panoptic segmentation. This extends to Diffusion Transformers only recently: ConceptAttention [ 16 ] shows DiT attention-layer projections yield sharper concept saliency than cross-attention alone; TRACE [ 17 ] shows diffusion models isolate object boundaries at a specific timestep, enabling spatial masks from internal attention. SGS extends this line of work to intra-image demographic fairness in multi-person scenes generated by T2I models.

FLUX [ 24 ] adopts this formulation, initializing generation from x 1 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and iteratively denoising via: x t − Δ ​ t = x t − Δ ​ t ⋅ v θ ​ ( x t , t , 𝐜 ) , x_{t-\Delta t}\;=\;x_{t}\;-\;\Delta t\cdot v_{\theta}(x_{t},\,t,\,\mathbf{c}), (1) where t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] decreases from 1 1 (pure noise) to 0 0 (clean image) over T T steps, Δ ​ t = 1 / T \Delta t=1/T , and 𝐜 \mathbf{c} is the encoded text condition [ 31 ] .

sections.heading: 3.2 Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT)
sections.text: The MM-DiT [ 10 ] architecture patchifies the noisy image latent x t ∈ ℝ H ​ W × d x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{HW\times d} , where H ​ W HW are the latent height and width and d d is the token dimension, into image tokens, concatenates them with text conditioning tokens 𝐜 \mathbf{c} [ 31 ] , and processes them through a stack of N N transformer layers, each applying joint image-text self-attention and a feedforward MLP. FLUX.1-Dev [ 24 ] uses N = 19 N{=}19 double-stream layers; SD3.5-Large [ 10 ] uses N = 38 N{=}38 joint transformer blocks.

sections.heading: 4 Methods
sections.text: SGS performs per-instance demographic steering within the standard rectified flow denoising loop, requiring no model fine-tuning, no trajectory inversion, and no external spatial layout specification. Crucially, instance masks are predicted directly from the MM-DiT’s attention features at a critical denoising step, rather than decoding the noisy latents for an external segmentor - which would be unreliable while the latent is still far from x 0 x_{0} , and redundant since these features are already computed by the base pass. Figure 1 illustrates the intuition behind our approach and Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete inference procedure. The denoising loop is divided into three phases governed by two hyperparameters: t start t_{\mathrm{start}} and t end t_{\mathrm{end}} . Before t start t_{\mathrm{start}} , generation proceeds without intervention. At t start t_{\mathrm{start}} , instance masks are extracted and cached. Between t start t_{\mathrm{start}} and t end t_{\mathrm{end}} , a separate steered forward pass is run per detected instance at each denoising step, and the predictions are spatially accumulated. After t end t_{\mathrm{end}} , standard denoising resumes to completion.

sections.heading: Segmentor Architecture.
sections.text: 𝐅 t \mathbf{F}_{t} is passed to a DETR-style [ 4 ] instance segmentor. The model comprises a three-layer CNN backbone that projects 𝐅 t ∈ ℝ H ​ W × 2 ​ H ​ W \mathbf{F}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{HW\times 2HW} into a spatial feature map, followed by a linear pixel projection that yields a sequence of pixel embeddings 𝐏 ∈ ℝ H ​ W × D e \mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{HW\times D_{e}} where D e D_{e} is the transformer embedding dimension. A set of N q N_{q} learnable instance queries 𝐐 ∈ ℝ N q × D e \mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{q}\times D_{e}} are refined by a L L -layer transformer decoder attending over 𝐏 \mathbf{P} . The denoising timestep t t is incorporated via a sinusoidal embedding concatenated to the input features, conditioning the segmentor on the noise level at which features were extracted. Each refined query produces three outputs via dedicated linear heads: conf i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , center i ∈ [ 0 , 32 ] 2 , M i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] 32 × 32 , \mathrm{conf}_{i}\in[0,1],\quad\mathrm{center}_{i}\in[0,32]^{2},\quad M_{i}\in[0,1]^{32\times 32}, (4) where conf i \mathrm{conf}_{i} is the instance confidence, center i \mathrm{center}_{i} is the predicted center coordinate, and M i M_{i} is the instance mask produced via a dot product between the query mask embedding and the pixel embedding sequence. Queries with confidence below a threshold τ \tau are discarded, yielding K ≤ N q K\leq N_{q} active instances. More details, along with the hyperparameters of the segmentor can be found in the supplementary material (Section B ).

sections.heading: Training Data.
sections.text: The segmentor is trained on a purpose-built dataset of 1440 1440 generated multi-person images spanning k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } k{\in}\{2,3,4,5\} persons across 9 scene types and 3 difficulty levels, with instance pseudo-labels produced by SAM2 [ 32 ] automatic mask generation. Full dataset details and the train/val split are provided in the supplementary material.

sections.text: The K K binary masks { M i } i = 1 K \{M_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} are cached and reused for all subsequent steps in the steering window without re-extraction. Each instance i i is assigned a target demographic attribute A i A_{i} by uniform sampling over the intersection of gender and racial attribute categories, which can be overridden at inference time to reflect user-specified fairness targets.

sections.heading: Model and Hardware Configurations.
sections.text: Our primary experiments use FLUX.1-Dev 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev in bfloat16 precision [ 19 ] on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU (48GB VRAM), with 21 denoising steps and a guidance scale of 4.5. To evaluate cross-architecture generalization, we additionally port SGS and all four baselines to SD3.5-Large 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-large in bfloat16 precision, run on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (39GB MIG slice), at 1024 × 1024 1024{\times}1024 resolution (its native training resolution) with 28 denoising steps and a guidance scale of 3.5. SGS’s instance-detection and per-instance steering mechanism (Section 4.1 , Section 3.3 ) makes no FLUX-specific assumption beyond the existence of a joint image-text self-attention map inside the denoising transformer, which SD3.5’s MM-DiT also provides. SD3.5-Large’s EA direction vectors live in the joint pooled embedding of its two CLIP encoders (CLIP-L and CLIP-G, concatenated to 2048-dim), rather than FLUX’s single 768-dim CLIP-L pooled space; T5 remains excluded from vector construction in both cases. sections.heading: Image Quality
sections.text: We report CLIP score [ 31 ] for prompt fidelity and aesthetic score delta ( A ​ e ​ s ​ Δ Aes\Delta ) relative to the unsteered baseline [ 33 ] . Face crops from the generated images are extracted using MTCNN [ 44 ] . Similar to prior works [ 39 , 41 ] , Demographic labels are produced by FairFace [ 20 ] detector, which we validate directly against known ground truth rather than assuming its accuracy (supplementary Section E ).

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol.
sections.text: We evaluate instance segmentation on a held-out test set of our dataset as described in Section 4.1 . The test set has n = 720 n{=}720 images across all k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } k\in\{2,3,4,5\} person counts and three difficulty levels. We report mean intersection-over-union (mIoU), average precision at IoU threshold (AP50) and average precision averaged over thresholds 50%–95% (AP50-95). Features are extracted at each denoising timestep t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] and we report performance across the full temporal sweep.

sections.heading: Architectural Comparison
sections.text: We compare four segmentation approaches of increasing supervisory complexity: K-Means (naive unsupervised baseline), Spectral clustering (following MaskDiffusion [ 21 ] ), CenterNet [ 48 ] (supervised, lightweight), and our DETR-style model (Section 4.1 ). TRACE [ 17 ] , which also extracts instance boundaries from diffusion self-attention maps, is a natural comparison, but its authors had not released training or inference code at submission time, precluding a faithful reproduction. Figure 3 reports performance across FLUX denoising timesteps. All methods improve as denoising progresses toward t ≈ 0.7 t{\approx}0.7 – 0.8 0.8 (step 4 of 21), then plateau or degrade as features shift toward fine-grained texture, confirming MM-DiT features become instance-discriminative at intermediate timesteps [ 17 , 38 ] ; together with the steering-window ablation (Section 5.4 ), this motivates t start = 4 t_{\mathrm{start}}{=}4 . DETR outperforms all baselines at every timestep, peaking at mIoU 0.664 , AP50 0.797 , AP50–95 0.416 (vs. CenterNet’s 0.618/0.762/0.337), reflecting the gap between supervised and unsupervised instance separation from DiT features. A DETR trained analogously on SD3.5-Large reaches a comparable peak (Section F ), so this timestep-localized discriminability is not FLUX-specific. Per-difficulty and qualitative detail: supplementary Sections C , G ; Section D shows the segmentor is not the bottleneck behind SGS’s steering accuracy at K ≤ 3 K{\leq}3 , but shows weaker performance at K = 4 K{=}4 .

sections.heading: Layer Bin Ablation.
sections.text: Performance improves monotonically from Bin 1 to Bin 4, reflecting the progression of spatial structure across MM-DiT layer depth - earlier layers encode coarse layout while later layers capture fine-grained instance boundaries. Concatenating Bins 3 and 4 achieves the best performance across all metrics (mIoU: 0.631, AP50: 0.747, AP50-95: 0.368, averaged across all timesteps), outperforming other bin configurations (full per-bin table in supplementary Section B ). sections.heading: Steering Window.
sections.text: We additionally sweep detection/steering start step t start ∈ { 2 , 4 , 6 } t_{\mathrm{start}}\in\{2,4,6\} and end step t end t_{\mathrm{end}} , with α = 2.0 \alpha{=}2.0 and λ = 4.0 \lambda{=}4.0 fixed (full grid and discussion in supplementary Section H , Table S6 ). Early detection ( t start = 2 t_{\mathrm{start}}{=}2 ) yields the highest steering accuracy but degrades background preservation and aesthetic quality, since MM-DiT features this early are insufficiently structured for reliable instance segmentation. Late detection ( t start = 6 t_{\mathrm{start}}{=}6 ) preserves background coherence but leaves too short a window to shift demographics effectively. We select t start = 4 t_{\mathrm{start}}{=}4 , t end = 10 t_{\mathrm{end}}{=}10 as our operating point for FLUX, balancing steering accuracy against background preservation and semantic drift. Similar Hyperparameter testing was done for SD3.5-Large and the results can be found in Section I .

sections.heading: 5.5 Benchmark Comparison
sections.text: We evaluate on 30 held-out WinoBias occupations (disjoint from the 10 used to fit EA’s direction vectors) × \times 5 prompt templates × \times k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 } k\in\{2,3,4\} × \times 10 seeds, on both FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Large (Section 5.1 ; full list in supplementary Section J ), yielding 4,500 images/method/architecture. We compare against Embedding Arithmetic [ 39 ] , SDID [ 25 ] , RespoDiff [ 40 ] , and FairImagen [ 12 ] ; DisCo [ 3 ] targets a related goal but requires fine-tuning and has no public implementation, precluding a faithful comparison. Each baseline was originally designed for UNet-based diffusion models; how we faithfully reimplemented them for MM-DiT is detailed in supplementary Section N . H i ​ x H_{ix} , CLIP, and A ​ e ​ s ​ Δ Aes\Delta are mean ± 95 % \pm 95\% CI (normal approximation); DR uses a percentile bootstrap (1000 resamples), since it is a population-level statistic rather than a per-image mean. Table 1 reports intra-image diversity ( H i ​ x H_{ix} ) against aggregate balance ( D ​ R DR ) on both architectures under one protocol. Since H i ​ x H_{ix} rewards any per-instance diversification, the two must be read jointly: global methods steer every person identically and so cannot raise intra-image diversity. Embedding Arithmetic reaches the lowest D ​ R r ​ a ​ c ​ e DR_{race} on both models, but its H i ​ x H_{ix} falls well below the unsteered baseline on both – a single demographic vector pushes everyone toward the same group, improving aggregate counts while erasing intra-image variation. SDID, RespoDiff, and FairImagen leave D ​ R DR close to baseline on both architectures, confirming that global latent and text-embedding projections do not transfer to either model’s joint-attention formulation. SGS is the only method to break this trade-off on both: highest H i ​ x H_{ix} by a wide margin, D ​ R r ​ a ​ c ​ e DR_{race} second only to EA, and prompt fidelity near baseline throughout. This pattern replicates on a second, architecturally distinct diffusion transformer, not just FLUX.

sections.heading: 5.6 Human Evaluation
sections.text: The metrics above rely on an automatic race/gender classifier (Section 5.1 ). To check that SGS’s gains are also visible to real people, not just to one automatic tool, we ran a small anonymous online study. Raters were shown two images side by side, one from SGS and one from a baseline, and asked which has more diverse people and which better matches the prompt, plus an overall preference. We collected 65 completed sessions (657 screens, 1971 judgments in total), comparing SGS against all five baselines. Table 2 shows the share of judgments that favored SGS. Raters preferred SGS on diversity by a wide margin against every baseline (88–90%, all differences statistically significant). On matching the prompt, results are mostly a tie, except SGS is clearly preferred over EA (89%). The overall preference question shows the same pattern: SGS is clearly favored over EA (76%) and roughly tied with the rest. Agreement between raters (Krippendorff’s alpha, where 1.0 means perfect agreement and 0 means no better than chance) was 0.73 for diversity – strong agreement – and lower, 0.43–0.44, for the more subjective faithfulness/preference questions, which is expected for personal-taste judgments. Full study design, recruiting, and per-question detail are in the supplementary material (Section O ). sections.text: Figure 2 ’s three occupations span orthogonal stereotype directions (nurses female-skewed; CEOs, farmers male-skewed), yet base outputs are homogeneous in all three. sections.heading: 5.8 Compute Cost
sections.text: Table 3 reports per-image denoising time measured on a single A6000 GPU (48GB) across 10 runs after 3 warm-up passes. EA introduces no additional forward passes and is within measurement noise of the baseline. SGS incurs a deterministic overhead of exactly K × ( t end − t start ) = 6 ​ K K\times(t_{\text{end}}-t_{\text{start}})=6K additional forward passes. For K = 3 K=3 the generation takes 14.6s versus 7.8s for the baseline. This cost is proportional to the scene complexity and can be reduced by narrowing the steering window at the expense of steering accuracy (Table S6 , supplementary Section H ).

sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: Three limitations bound the current system. First, segmentor accuracy degrades for k ≥ 4 k{\geq}4 persons in heavily occluded scenes, this also impacts the steering accuracy. Second, the per-instance forward pass introduces a compute overhead proportional to K K . Batching would reduce wall-clock time at the cost of VRAM, a trade-off we could not explore within our hardware budget. Third, SGS applies steering regardless of prompt intent; a query such as “four male doctors” will still redistribute demographics. A lightweight prompt parser that zeroes the steering signal for explicitly constrained slots could address this.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented SGS, a per-instance demographic steering framework for multi-person T2I generation requiring no fine-tuning, inversion, or layout input. Global steering improves aggregate balance only by driving intra-image diversity below the unsteered baseline; SGS is the only evaluated method to break this trade-off, raising intersectional entropy to 0.794 (from 0.524) on FLUX.1-Dev and to 0.832 (from 0.549) on SD3.5-Large, while recovering near-best aggregate balance and preserving semantic coherence on both architectures. Per-instance spatial steering thus emerges as a necessary step toward fair multi-person text-to-image generation, generalizing across architecturally distinct diffusion transformers rather than being a property of any single model.

sections.heading: Appendix A Segmentor - Training Dataset Details
sections.text: The segmentor is trained on a purpose-built dataset of 1440 generated multi-person images spanning k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } k\in\{2,3,4,5\} persons across 9 scene types and 3 difficulty levels. The 9 scene types are: market, bus stop, city landmark, outdoor concert, train station, backyard barbecue, city park, street food fair, and mountain trail . Difficulty encodes camera framing and occlusion: easy uses a wide shot with subjects standing apart facing the camera; medium uses a medium shot with subjects side by side; hard uses tight close-up shots with partial occlusion among subjects. All images were generated using FLUX.1-Dev at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution with guidance scale 4.5 and 21 denoising steps.

sections.heading: Train/val/test split
sections.text: The 1440 training images are split into 80% training and 20% validation images, stratified by k k and difficulty level. The test set ( n = 720 n{=}720 ) is generated from a disjoint set of 9 out-of-distribution scene types with different framing protocol to evaluate generalisation beyond the training distribution.

sections.heading: Pseudo-label generation
sections.text: Instance segmentation masks are produced by SAM2 [ 32 ] automatic mask generation applied to each generated image. Predicted masks are filtered by minimum area and matched to ground-truth person count k k via Hungarian matching on mask centroid distance. Duplicate predictions with pairwise IoU > 0.5 >0.5 are suppressed by retaining the higher confidence mask.

sections.heading: Appendix B Segmentor - Architecture
sections.text: We describe each component of the instance segmentor with exact hyper-parameter values as used in all reported experiments.

sections.heading: Input Features.
sections.text: The segmentor receives the binned self-attention feature map 𝐅 t \mathbf{F}_{t} , formed by concatenating layer bins b = 3 b{=}3 and b = 4 b{=}4 of the MM-DiT self-attention at the detection timestep t start t_{\mathrm{start}} . Features are min-max normalized per channel before being passed to the backbone. This choice of bins is itself the result of an ablation (Table S1 , moved here from the main paper’s Section 5.3 for space): performance improves monotonically from Bin 1 to Bin 4 as layer depth increases, and concatenating Bins 3+4 outperforms every single-bin or other-pair configuration tested. sections.heading: Timestep Conditioning
sections.text: The continuous FLUX timestep t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] is encoded via a sinusoidal embedding followed by a learned linear projection with SiLU activation. The embedding is spatially broadcast and concatenated channel-wise to 𝐅 t \mathbf{F}_{t} before the backbone, conditioning the segmentor on the noise level at which features were extracted.

sections.heading: CNN Backbone
sections.text: Three ConvBnReLU blocks (Conv2d, BatchNorm2d, ReLU, same-padding) progressively compress the high-dimensional attention channels into a compact spatial feature map while preserving the 32 × 32 32{\times}32 resolution throughout. A final 1 × 1 1{\times}1 convolution projects to the transformer embedding dimension D e = 128 D_{e}{=}128 , yielding pixel embeddings 𝐏 ∈ ℝ 1,024 × 128 \mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{1{,}024\times 128} after spatial flattening.

sections.heading: Transformer decoder.
sections.text: N q = 8 N_{q}{=}8 learnable instance queries are refined by L = 2 L{=}2 decoder layers. Each layer applies self-attention among the queries, cross-attention from queries to 𝐏 \mathbf{P} , and a two-layer FFN with GELU activation, all with residual connections and LayerNorm ( H = 4 H{=}4 attention heads throughout).

sections.heading: Output heads.
sections.text: Each refined query produces three outputs via dedicated linear heads: a scalar confidence conf i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \mathrm{conf}_{i}\in[0,1] a center coordinate center i ∈ [ 0 , 32 ] 2 \mathrm{center}_{i}\in[0,32]^{2} , and an instance mask M i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] 32 × 32 M_{i}\in[0,1]^{32\times 32} computed as a dot-product between a per-query mask embedding and 𝐏 \mathbf{P} , reshaped to 32 × 32 32\times 32 . center i \mathrm{center}_{i} is used only during training to stabilize the Hungarian matching.

sections.heading: Inference
sections.text: Queries with conf i < τ = 0.5 \mathrm{conf}_{i}<\tau{=}0.5 are discarded and the retained masks are binarized at > 0.5 >0.5 , yielding K ≤ 8 K\leq 8 binary instance masks. No NMS is applied - K K is determined by the confidence threshold.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: The model is trained for 50 epochs with Adam ( lr = 10 − 4 \mathrm{lr}{=}10^{-4} , batch size 8, 5 linear warm-up epochs). The 1,440 training images are split 80/20 into 1,152 training and 288 validation samples, stratified by k k and difficulty. Loss weights: w c = 2.0 w_{c}{=}2.0 , w m = 2.0 w_{m}{=}2.0 . The complete segmentor has 1.2M parameters, lightweight relative to the FLUX DiT backbone it operates on. sections.text: Figure 4 breaks down DETR segmentor performance across scene difficulty ( left ) and person count K K ( right ). AP50 remains consistently high across all cases, while AP50-95 drops substantially, indicating that instances are reliably detected but mask boundaries lack the precision required at stricter IoU thresholds. This gap widens at higher K K , where spatial competition between instances further degrades boundary delineation. sections.heading: Appendix E Classifier Validation
sections.text: All race/gender numbers in this paper depend on one automatic tool, FairFace [ 20 ] . To read demographics off a generated face, before trusting it, we check how accurate it actually is against a set of images where the true demographic is known for certain, and we also check two other classifiers (a CLIP [ 31 ] zero-shot classifier, and DeepFace [ 34 ] ) for comparison.

sections.heading: Building a set of images with known demographics.
sections.text: We generate images where every person in the group is asked for the same demographic (e.g. “a group of three Black women”), so the prompt itself has a cue for every face in that image. This is done for both FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Large, across all 8 race × \times gender combinations and group sizes k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 } k\in\{2,3,4\} . We keep only images where a face detector actually finds exactly k k faces, to avoid mixing in blank or wrong-count images; this leaves 1,832 individual face crops with a known-correct label.

sections.heading: Results.

sections.heading: Do the three classifiers agree with each other?
sections.text: Separately from whether each classifier is correct, we check how often the three classifiers agree with each other (Krippendorff’s alpha, where 1.0 means perfect agreement and 0 means no better than chance). sections.heading: Steering window
sections.text: Early detection and steering at t start = 2 t_{\mathrm{start}}{=}2 yields the highest steering accuracy across all end points but produces consistently negative aesthetic deltas and poor background preservation (LPIPS bg ≤ 0.759 {}_{\mathrm{bg}}{\leq}0.759 ), indicating that MM-DiT features at step 2 are insufficiently structured for reliable instance segmentation, causing the steering signal to leak beyond the intended mask regions. Late detection and steering at t start = 6 t_{\mathrm{start}}{=}{6} preserves background coherence well (LPIPS bg ≥ 0.956 {}_{\mathrm{bg}}{\geq}0.956 ) but achieves substantially lower steering accuracy ( Acc race ≤ 0.594 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{race}}{\leq}0.594 , Acc gender ≤ 0.652 \mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{gender}}{\leq}0.652 ), as the remaining steering window is too short to shift demographics effectively. t start = 4 t_{\mathrm{start}}{=}4 achieves the best balance across all metrics: extending the end step from 8 to 10 improves steering accuracy (0.632 → \to 0.708 race, 0.744 → \to 0.757 gender) with only marginal reductions in background preservation, while further extension to t end = 12 t_{\mathrm{end}}{=}12 or 14 14 offers diminishing accuracy gains at the cost of increasing semantic drift. We therefore select t start = 4 t_{\mathrm{start}}{=}4 and t end = 10 t_{\mathrm{end}}{=}10 as our operating point, corresponding to steps 4–10 of the 21-step denoising trajectory.

sections.heading: Appendix L Extended Qualitative Analysis
sections.text: Figure 7 presents an extended qualitative comparison across four occupations spanning both stereotype directions and three person counts k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 } k\in\{2,3,4\} . Occupations include two female-dominated professions (Nurse, Housekeeping) and two male-dominated professions (Sheriffs, Construction Workers).

sections.heading: Baseline.
sections.text: Across all four occupations and all values of k k , the unsteered baseline produces demographically homogeneous outputs that reflect occupational stereotypes; Nurses and Housekeepers are consistently female-presenting or White, while Sheriffs and Construction workers are consistently male-presenting and White. This homogeneity persists regardless of k k , confirming that the stereotyping is driven by the text prompt rather than any scene composition effect introduced by specifying multiple persons.

sections.heading: SGS across person counts.
sections.text: SGS consistently produces intersectional demographic diversity across all k k values. At k = 2 k=2 , each pair contains two persons steered to distinct intersectional targets– for example, a Black male nurse is paired with an Asian female nurse, or an Indian male housekeeper paired with an Asian female housekeeper. At k = 3 k=3 and k = 4 k=4 , the segmentor reliably separates all persons and assigns independent demographic vectors to each, with the resulting groups spanning multiple racial categories and both genders within the same image. The consistency across k k values demonstrates that the instance segmentor remains reliable as scene complexity increases.

sections.heading: Occupational context preservation.
sections.text: A key requirement of practical fairness steering is that demographic edits do not disrupt occupational cues. Across all conditions, SGS preserves the visual markers of each profession: nurses retain scrubs and stethoscopes, sheriffs retain badges and hats, housekeepers retain aprons, and construction workers retain safety helmets and reflective vests. This confirms that the spatially gated steering is confined to person regions via the instance masks, preventing demographic steering from leaking into occupational attire or scene background.

sections.heading: Appendix M Qualitative Comparison – SD3.5-Large
sections.text: Figure 8 repeats the main paper’s qualitative comparison (Figure 2 ) on SD3.5-Large, across four prompts and all five baselines. Images from Base, EA, FairImagen, RespoDiff, and SDID remain demographically homogeneous or only mildly shifted across all four scenes, while SGS diversifies every scene independently per person while preserving occupational context (aprons, rice-field setting, formal attire). This confirms the pattern shown quantitatively in Table 1 holds qualitatively on a second architecture as well. Figure 7 : Extended qualitative comparison across four occupations and three person counts k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 } k\in\{2,3,4\} . Left : baseline FLUX outputs. Right : SGS outputs. Rows show female-dominant (Nurses, Housekeepers) and male-dominant (Sheriffs, Construction Workers) professions. Baseline outputs are demographically homogeneous across all k k values and both stereotype directions. SGS consistently produces intersectional demographic diversity — each person within the same scene is steered to a distinct demographic target — while also preserving occupational context (uniform, apron, badge, hard hat) and scene coherence across all conditions. Performance is consistent across k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 } k\in\{2,3,4\} , demonstrating that the segmentor reliably separates and independently steers two, three, and four persons within the same image. Base, EA, FairImagen, RespoDiff, and SDID remain homogeneous or only mildly shifted across all four prompts; SGS independently diversifies each detected person while preserving occupational context.

sections.heading: Appendix N Baseline Adaptation to Diffusion Transformers
sections.text: FairImagen [ 12 ] , SDID [ 25 ] , and RespoDiff [ 40 ] were each designed and released against older UNet-based diffusion models – FairImagen against SD1.5 and SDXL, RespoDiff against SDXL, and SDID against a UNet-based Stable Diffusion pipeline – where generation is driven by a single-stream convolutional UNet with cross-attention to a text encoder. FLUX and SD3.5-Large instead use a Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT, Section 3.2 ): image and text tokens are processed jointly through a stack of self-attention blocks, with no UNet and no single bottleneck layer. None of the three methods’ released implementations run on this architecture family as-is. We faithfully reimplemented each method’s core mechanism for MM-DiT, verified directly against its own released code, rather than mechanically porting UNet-specific hooks.

sections.heading: FairImagen.
sections.text: The original method operates on the model’s pooled text-conditioning vector. For each demographic group g g , it defines an empirical bias direction ν g = 1 | X ( g ) | ​ ∑ E ¯ p ∈ X ( g ) E ¯ p − E ¯ , \nu_{g}=\frac{1}{|X^{(g)}|}\sum_{\bar{E}_{p}\in X^{(g)}}\bar{E}_{p}-\bar{E}, (13) and obtains a projector P P by solving min P ⊤ ​ P = I − Tr ⁡ ( P ⊤ ​ Σ X ​ P ) + λ ​ ∥ B ​ P ∥ F 2 , \min_{P^{\top}P=I}\;-\mathrm{Tr}(P^{\top}\Sigma_{X}P)+\lambda\lVert BP\rVert_{F}^{2}, (14) where B = Z ⊤ ​ X ∈ ℝ G × D B=Z^{\top}X\in\mathbb{R}^{G\times D} collects the per-group mean directions and Z ∈ { 0 , 1 } n × G Z\in\{0,1\}^{n\times G} is a one-hot group indicator; P P thus spans the top-variance directions within the null space of the group-dependent signal B B . At inference, the projector is applied orthogonally to the pooled embedding, E ¯ p ′ = P ​ P ⊤ ​ E ¯ p \bar{E}_{p}^{\prime}=PP^{\top}\bar{E}_{p} , before it conditions the UNet. MM-DiT models expose an analogous pooled conditioning vector alongside their token-level sequence conditioning, so we fit and apply this same projector on this real pooled vector, leaving the token sequence untouched.

sections.text: The original method learns a single concept offset c ∈ ℝ D c\in\mathbb{R}^{D} per demographic direction by c ∗ = arg ⁡ min c ​ ∑ x , y ∼ 𝒟 ∑ t ∼ [ 0 , T ] ∥ ϵ − ϵ θ ​ ( x t + , t , π ⁡ ( y − ) , c ) ∥ 2 , c^{*}=\arg\min_{c}\sum_{x,y\sim\mathcal{D}}\sum_{t\sim[0,T]}\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t}^{+},t,\pi(y^{-}),c)\rVert^{2}, (15) where x + x^{+} is an image generated from a concept-inclusive prompt and y − y^{-} is the same prompt with the concept term removed, with the base model ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} kept frozen throughout. At inference, the offset is added directly to the UNet’s image-latent bottleneck activation, h ← h + c h\leftarrow h+c , a single injection point on the image side of the network. MM-DiT has no UNet bottleneck to target, so we carry the same design principle over: the learned offset is added to the hidden state of one representative block within the joint-transformer stack, preserving a single image-side injection point rather than broadcasting the offset into the text-token stream.

Our first attempt at reimplementing this for MM-DiT broadcast the same residual across every block of the joint-transformer stack; this reliably broke generation, producing incoherent output regardless of prompt or seed. Injecting the residual at a single representative block instead resolved this and produced coherent, steerable output. This also brings the reimplementation closer to the original method’s own single-bottleneck design than the all-block version we started from.

sections.heading: Shared adaptations.
sections.text: All three methods are applied only to the conditional half of the classifier-free-guidance batch, never the unconditional branch, consistent with how each was originally deployed. Training uses each target architecture’s own native noise parametrization and scheduler rather than a generic substitute.

sections.heading: Code Availability.
sections.text: Reference implementations of all three adapted baselines are included in the supplementary code ( baselines/flux/ and baselines/sd35/ ): fairimagen.py , sdid.py , and respodiff.py , each containing the fit/training function and manipulation function described above with inline comments matching this section. SGS itself is in sgs/ (FLUX) and sgs_sd3/ (SD3.5-Large).

sections.heading: Appendix O Human Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: Automatic demographic classifiers may not fully capture how a human observer perceives diversity, prompt fidelity and preference. So we conducted a blind pairwise human evaluation comparing SGS against five baselines (Baseline, EA, FairImagen, RespoDiff and SDID) across 33 scenes spanning WinoBias occupations at K ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 } K\in\{2,3,4\} people per image, using a fixed seed per scene shared across all six methods. Each rater was shown two images side by side from the same scene, generated by two different methods (one always SGS), with method identity withheld (labeled only ’Image A’/’Image B’) and left – right placement randomized per pair. For each pair, raters answered three questions (refer Figure 9 ): 1. Which image shows more diversity in race and gender? 2. Which image better matches the caption above? 3. Given a choice, which image would you prefer? The first two questions offered a three way choice (Image A / about equal / Image B), while the last was a forced binary choice used to obtain a holistic preference signal. Each participants rated 10 pairs, two per comparison, ensuring balanced coverage across all five comparisons within a session. Sessions in which a rater selected the identical response to every question throughout were excluded prior to analysis. For each comparison and question, we report the percentage of judgments preferring SGS (ties counted as half a preference) with a 95% Wilson score confidence interval and a two-sided exact binomial test against the 50% chance level (ties excluded from the significance test), alongside Krippendorff’s α \alpha (nominal) as a measure of inter-rater reliability [ 23 ] ; results are reported in Table 2 . Figure 9 : The human evaluation interface. Raters see a captioned imagepair with method identity and position blinded, and answer three questions per pair: perceived diversity, prompt faithfulness, and overall preference.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.29651v1 [cs.CV] 21 Oct 2026 Spatially Gated Demographic Steering for Debiasing Multi-Person Text-to-Image Generation Venkatesh Thirugnana Sambandham Affiliation: Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt Affiliation: Ingolstadt, Germany Email: venkatesh.thirugnanasambandham@thi.de Torsten Schön Affiliation: Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt Affiliation: Ingolstadt, Germany Email: torsten.schoen@thi.de Abstract Text-to-Image models reproduce societal stereotypes, and existing mitigation applies one demographic correction to the whole scene. In multi-person scene generation this creates a trade-off: global steering improves aggregate balance only by homogenizing the people within an image. Steering-based methods like Embedding Arithmetic drive the intra-image diversity below the unsteered baseline. Text- and latent-projection approaches shift the aggregate skew with only marginal gains in intra-image diversity. We present Spatially Gated Steering (SGS), which steers the demographics of each person independently by extracting per-person masks from the Diffusion Transformer’s (DiT) internal attention maps at a critical denoising timestep and applying a distinct demographic vector within each mask for the remaining steps. SGS needs no fine-tuning, inversion or layout specifications, and uses a lightweight segmentor over frozen DiT attention features to localize subjects at early timesteps. On skewed occupational prompts, SGS reaches high intra-image racial and gender diversity while keeping aggregate balance competitive and image quality near baseline, a result we validate on two architecturally distinct diffusion transformers, FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Large. Codebase and model weights are available at https://github.com/cvims/spatially-gated-steering 1 Introduction Text-to-Image (T2I) generation has transformed digital content creation, yet foundational models such as FLUX [ 24 ] and Stable Diffusion [ 10 ] systematically reproduce societal stereotypes [ 9 ] . Gender-neutral prompts like a carpenter yield predominantly male-presenting images; a nurse yields predominantly female-presenting images [ 28 ] . Studies show these outputs shift user beliefs about real-world distributions [ 14 ] , making fairness mitigation essential for responsible deployment. Figure 1 : SGS intuition. The base trajectory (black) reaches x 0 base x_{0}^{\text{base}} in a stereotyped region of p data p_{\text{data}} ; global mitigation [ 39 ] (brown dashed) shifts it to one alternative mode. SGS instead intercepts at x start x_{\text{start}} , extracts per-person masks, and steers each individual independently (orange/blue dashed) toward distinct demographic attractors within the same image x 0 x_{0} . Several mitigation strategies have been proposed and they operate at different levels of the diffusion pipeline [ 37 ] : They modify the text embeddings [ 39 , 6 , 43 , 22 ] or fine-tune model weights [ 13 , 36 ] to shift the aggregate output distribution. While effective for scenes with a single person, global mitigation methods share a fundamental limitation: They apply identical steering to every person in a scene. A prompt like ”a group of nurses” receives one demographic vector, pushing all the persons in the image in the same direction and failing to diversify individuals independently. Figure 2 : Qualitative comparison across three profession types spanning different stereotype directions. Prompts contain no demographic descriptors. Base is demographically homogeneous; EA shifts everyone uniformly; FairImagen is statistically indistinguishable from baseline on FLUX; SGS steers each instance toward a distinct intersectional target while preserving occupational context and scene coherence. Rightmost column: segmentation masks (nearest-neighbor upsampled from 32 × 32 32\times 32 ) with assigned demographic labels. This limitation is not merely theoretical: Wan and Chang [41] show that multi-person prompts expose a distinct, compounding class of bias that single-subject evaluations cannot capture. Co-occurring subjects amplify stereotypes even when the same model behaves anti-stereotypically on single-person prompts. Attempts to address this gap remain limited. Existing approaches either rewrite the generation prompt with a single corrective signal applied to the whole scene [ 41 , 8 ] , optimize demographic distributions at the aggregate level without per-instance control [ 18 ] , or require an explicit spatial layout as input [ 7 ] . To the best of our knowledge, no existing method localizes individuals from the model’s own internal representations and applies independent demographic steering, to achieve intra-image diversity. Figure 1 illustrates this gap: while global mitigation shifts all persons uniformly toward a single demographic mode, our approach steers each individual independently through their spatial mask, reaching distinct attractors within p data p_{\text{data}} in a single denoising pass. We introduce Spatially Gated Steering (SGS) , a framework for per-instance demographic steering in multi-person T2I scene generation. SGS operates by 1) Identifying and generating the masks of instances of people during the intermediate denoising steps using a lightweight detector, 2) Steering the demographics of the detected individuals, while also maintaining concept coherence. Our contributions are as follows: • A trade-off in multi-person fairness. Global mitigation faces an inherent tension: improving aggregate balance requires collapsing intra-image diversity, sometimes below the unsteered baseline. Since any per-instance diversification trivially raises intra-image entropy, the meaningful result is high entropy at a competitive aggregate balance. SGS reaches high intra-image diversity with a competitive aggregate balance by steering per-instance without fine-tuning, flow-inversion or layout. • Instance segmentation from DiT features. We show that self-attention maps of DiTs at a critical denoising timestep encode spatially separable person instances, and train a lightweight DETR-style [ 4 ] segmentor on these frozen features that isolates individuals across crowd sizes and scene complexities. • Benchmark and analysis. We introduce a benchmark measuring fairness along both intra-image diversity and aggregate deviation, surfacing the homogenization failure mode of global methods and showing SGS is strong on both axes, on both FLUX.1-Dev and SD3.5-Large. 2 Related Works Bias and Fairness in Text-to-Image Models. T2I models have been extensively shown to amplify demographic stereotypes encoded in training data, producing outputs skewed by gender, race and cultural identity across a wide range of prompt types [ 1 , 5 , 35 , 28 ] . Beyond documenting these skews, a parallel line of work formalizes their measurement: Dehdashtian et al. [ 9 ] quantify stereotypical attributes in the generated set and trace their origin within the model, reporting that even high-fidelity systems such as FLUX retain strong stereotypical predispositions. Mitigation strategies operate at different points in the generation pipeline: prompt engineering injects demographic descriptors at inference [ 11 , 2 , 43 ] , embedding manipulation steers text representations prior to image generation [ 39 , 6 , 22 , 25 , 26 , 15 ] , and parameter-efficient fine-tuning edits model weights to shift output distributions [ 13 , 36 ] . Park et al.’s Entanglement-Free Attention [ 30 ] shares our goal of preserving non-target attributes during bias mitigation, training cross-attention predictors under a mask-constrained regularization loss so background edits are suppressed. However, like other global methods, it applies one scene-level attribute correction rather than steering each person independently. Despite this breadth, all existing methods treat the generated image as a single unit, applying one steering signal to the entire scene. This is sufficient when a prompt produces one person, but breaks down entirely for multi-person scenes where distinct individuals require independent control. Multi-person Bias and Instance-level Control. This breakdown in multi-subject generation is primarily driven by semantic leakage, a phenomenon where the attention mechanisms of diffusion architectures inadvertently blend the visual and demographic features of different subjects during the denoising trajectory. Wan and Chang [41] demonstrate the consequences of this at scale: their Paired Stereotype Test shows that over 74% of DALL-E 3 images depicting two individuals with contrastive social identities display gender-occupational biases, even when the same model produces anti-stereotypical outputs for single-person prompts. Jung et al. [18] propose a Multi-Group Proportional Representation metric to measure and optimize demographic distributions across intersectional groups, but operate at the aggregate level without per-instance control. A related direction targets stereotypes that emerge from the co-occurrence of multiple concepts within a single prompt: Zhou et al. [47] show that pairing a demographic descriptor with an unrelated object can induce stereotypical associations invisible to single-concept audits, mitigated via a trained Sensitive Transformer that constrains the output distribution toward a stereotype-free target. This targets a distinct problem from ours, stereotyped associations between a subject and its surrounding context, corrected globally over the whole generation, rather than diversifying multiple people already explicitly present in a scene. Training-free inference methods such as Bounded Attention [ 7 ] attempt to prevent semantic leakage by confining attention flows within manually predefined spatial bounding boxes, but rely on rigid user-provided layouts rather than organic scene composition. Reinforcement learning approaches such as DisCo [ 3 ] directly fine-tune models to penalize intra-image facial similarity, but use face similarity as a proxy for demographic diversity rather than steering specific attribute vectors, and incur significant computational overhead. Global steering techniques such as Embedding Arithmetic [ 39 ] modify text embeddings uniformly, which fundamentally fails to produce heterogeneous intra-image diversity. Diffusion Features for Spatial Understanding. Intermediate diffusion activations encode rich spatial structure without additional training: DIFT [ 38 ] shows mid-denoising U-Net features support zero-shot dense correspondence; ODISE [ 42 ] uses Stable Diffusion U-Net features for open-vocabulary panoptic segmentation. This extends to Diffusion Transformers only recently: ConceptAttention [ 16 ] shows DiT attention-layer projections yield sharper concept saliency than cross-attention alone; TRACE [ 17 ] shows diffusion models isolate object boundaries at a specific timestep, enabling spatial masks from internal attention. SGS extends this line of work to intra-image demographic fairness in multi-person scenes generated by T2I models. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Rectified Flow Denoising Rectified flow [ 27 ] learns a velocity field v θ v_{\theta} (a neural network with parameters θ \theta ) that transports samples from a Gaussian noise distribution to the data distribution along approximately straight trajectories. FLUX [ 24 ] adopts this formulation, initializing generation from x 1 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and iteratively denoising via: x t − Δ ​ t = x t − Δ ​ t ⋅ v θ ​ ( x t , t , 𝐜 ) , x_{t-\Delta t}\;=\;x_{t}\;-\;\Delta t\cdot v_{\theta}(x_{t},\,t,\,\mathbf{c}), (1) where t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] decreases from 1 1 (pure noise) to 0 0 (clean image) over T T steps, Δ ​ t = 1 / T \Delta t=1/T , and 𝐜 \mathbf{c} is the encoded text condition [ 31 ] . 3.2 Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT) The MM-DiT [ 10 ] architecture patchifies the noisy image latent x t ∈ ℝ H ​ W × d x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{HW\times d} , where H ​ W HW are the latent height and width and d d is the token dimension, into image tokens, concatenates them with text conditioning tokens 𝐜 \mathbf{c} [ 31 ] , and processes them through a stack of N N transformer layers, each applying joint image-text self-attention and a feedforward MLP.
